title: Jio's 1,600-Satellite Plan Gets Green Light as Starlink's India Launch Stalls
excerpt: IN-SPACe has cleared Reliance Jio's low-Earth-orbit constellation as technically sound, while Starlink, JioSatcom and Eutelsat OneWeb await Home Ministry security clearances before switching on commercial services.
body:
• IN-SPACe, ISRO and the Department of Telecommunications have found Reliance Jio's plan for a 1,600-satellite low-Earth-orbit constellation "technically sound" — clearing the way for New Delhi to back the project internationally.
  • Jio's network would deliver 4.5–5 terabits per second over India from satellites at 650 km altitude — topping Starlink's approved 600 Gbps and Amazon's proposed 3 Tbps — with defence payloads under discussion.
  • Starlink, JioSatcom and Eutelsat OneWeb all hold licences but cannot start commercial services until Home Ministry security clearances complete; no timeline has been given.
  • What it means for NRIs: families in underserved regions could see satellite broadband as early as late 2026 if spectrum clears on schedule; Jio's own fleet targets test flights in September 2027.

Reliance Jio has taken a major step toward building India's first homegrown satellite-internet network, winning a technical green light from the country's space regulator for a 1,600-satellite constellation designed to rival Elon Musk's Starlink — even as Starlink itself remains stuck in India's licensing queue.

A joint panel of the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe), the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the Wireless Planning and Coordination wing of the Department of Telecommunications assessed Jio's proposal as "technically sound" and comparable to global systems such as Starlink, the Economic Times reported in July. The clearance lets New Delhi back Jio internationally as it seeks orbital slots and files with the International Telecommunication Union.

The plan, in numbers

Jio's proposed constellation would place about 1,600 satellites at an altitude of roughly 650 km — just above Starlink's 550 km and Amazon Leo's 630 km, in a band that analysts say offers cleaner orbital slots, according to Advanced Television. Unlike traditional geostationary satellites parked 36,000 km above the Earth, low-Earth-orbit satellites sit close enough to deliver fast, low-latency connections.

https://x.com/business_today/status/2108392225243885628

The headline number is capacity: Jio projects 4.5 to 5 terabits per second of throughput over India, roughly 100–150 Gb/s per satellite — topping both Starlink (about 600 Gbps approved) and Amazon Leo (3 Tbps proposed, not yet authorized), according to Outlook Business.

The project also carries strategic weight. IN-SPACe has flagged the constellation's defence value, and talks are underway about hosting defence-related payloads on some of the satellites — a sign that India wants sovereign control of critical connectivity rather than depending on foreign-owned networks.

Starlink waits at the gate

Starlink, JioSatcom and Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb have all secured operator licences from the Department of Telecommunications, and Starlink received its IN-SPACe authorization in July. But none can switch on commercial services until security assessments run by the Ministry of Home Affairs are complete — and the government has given no timeline.

Minister of State for Communications Chandra Sekhar Pemmasani told PTI this week that the department has issued licences and provisional spectrum to all three companies, and that the pending clearance "has nothing to do with one company."

"Now the issue is pending with MHA for security clearance. As soon as it is cleared, they will get it. It has nothing to do with one company."

— Chandra Sekhar Pemmasani, Minister of State for Communications

Musk has publicly accused unnamed business interests of blocking Starlink to preserve "a monopolistic chokehold" on the Indian market — comments widely read as aimed at Reliance chairman Mukesh Ambani. The telecom ministry rejected the allegation as baseless, saying India's framework is "fair and non-discriminatory." When Musk asked on X, "Is Ambani the real boss of India?", Congress leader Rahul Gandhi replied: "Welcome to India, Elon. Wait till you discover the other guy."

A crowded runway

Industry executives cited by the Economic Times say commercial satellite services could begin as early as November or December 2026 once spectrum is allotted — roughly a month after allotment.

Jio's own timeline is longer and more ambitious. On paper, the company targets test flights in September 2027, service in India from early 2028, 400–450 satellites by 2030 and the full 1,600-satellite fleet by 2035, according to Advanced Television. But major questions remain unanswered: no satellite manufacturing, launch, ground-station or terminal contracts have been announced, and analysts note that India currently lacks the launch cadence a 1,600-satellite build demands. At the company's annual general meeting, Akash Ambani described the sovereign constellation as something Jio is "evaluating," pursuing a dual approach of leasing capacity from partners while building its own.

"Unfortunately, we are being blocked by certain oligarchs in order to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people. You can guess who they are… This is a crime against the people of India!"

— Elon Musk, in a post on X

What to watch

The next milestones are regulatory: the Home Ministry's security clearances and the spectrum-allocation rules. For NRIs with family in India's remote regions — mountain villages, islands, border areas where fiber and towers are impractical — the prize is affordable high-speed connectivity. Whether it arrives first via Starlink's waiting fleet or Jio's sovereign constellation will be one of Indian telecom's defining races of the next decade.
